title: The JVM default timezone is sent as the PostgreSQL 'TimeZone' startup parameter - on a host whose zone is 'Asia/Saigon' every database connection is refused
actual: The PostgreSQL JDBC driver (42.7.11) adds a startup parameter TimeZone = TimeZone.getDefault().getID() on every connection (ConnectionFactoryImpl.getParametersForStartup / createPostgresTimeZone). PostgreSQL validates that parameter against pg_timezone_names, which does NOT contain backward-compatibility links such as 'Asia/Saigon' - the connection is refused with FATAL: invalid value for parameter "TimeZone": "Asia/Saigon". No service, compose file or k8s manifest pins TZ, so the JVM inherits the host timezone. Measured against postgres:16 with the production driver: default (Asia/Saigon) -> FAILED; -Duser.timezone=UTC -> CONNECTED (server TimeZone = UTC); -Duser.timezone=Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh -> CONNECTED; -Duser.timezone=Asia/Saigon -> FAILED. The same failure produced 416 errors in the Testcontainers integration suites.
expected: The platform connects to PostgreSQL regardless of the host timezone, and the build is reproducible on any developer machine.
trigger: Any deployment whose JVM resolves the default timezone to a backward-compatibility zone id. The project's own developer machines resolve to Asia/Saigon.
root_cause: The JVM timezone is unpinned, and the value is sent to the server as a startup parameter that PostgreSQL validates strictly.
consequences: Total outage of all twelve database-backed services on such a host: no connection can be established, so the application context never starts. The entire Testcontainers suite fails, so the defect is invisible in CI (ubuntu-latest runs UTC) but blocks every developer on a non-UTC machine.
remediation: Pin user.timezone=UTC for the surefire/failsafe forks and for the Jib-produced images; document the requirement in the deployment runbook. Implemented in this audit.
regression_test: The proof program production-audit/tests/contracts/TzProof.java connects to a real postgres:16 container with and without -Duser.timezone and asserts the outcome.
remediation_applied: pom.xml: surefire + failsafe systemPropertyVariables user.timezone=UTC; Jib jvmFlags -Duser.timezone=UTC.
verification_evidence: TzProof runtime comparison (Asia/Saigon -> FAILED, UTC -> CONNECTED); the full Testcontainers suites went from 416 errors to green.

title: tax-service soft-delete contradicts its own test - the module's build was RED, and the fleet had two different soft-delete attribution conventions
actual: TaxClassServiceImpl.delete used auditorAware.getCurrentAuditor().orElse("system"), so a destructive configuration change was attributed to a pseudo-actor. The module's own test TaxClassServiceImplTest.deleteRequiresAuditor asserted that the delete must fail when no auditor is resolvable - the test failed on every build ("Expecting code to raise a throwable"). The fleet had two conventions: promotion-service used orElseThrow(), while favourite-service, product-service (3 sites) and tax-service (2 sites) used orElse("system").
expected: One convention across the fleet: a destructive soft-delete must be attributable to a real actor, and the tax-service implementation must match its own test.
trigger: An administrative delete performed by a caller for which the AuditorAware cannot resolve a principal.
root_cause: Two incompatible conventions coexisted and the implementation drifted away from the test that specifies the contract.
consequences: The build was red on every run - a release blocker in itself. Beyond that, a destructive tax-configuration delete could be attributed to 'system' instead of the administrator who performed it, degrading the audit trail.
remediation: Align tax-service with the strict convention (orElseThrow) that promotion-service and the tax test already encode. The fleet-wide convention for the remaining .orElse("system") sites is tracked as a follow-up task.
remediation_applied: TaxClassServiceImpl.delete and TaxRateServiceImpl.delete now use orElseThrow().
verification_evidence: tax-service module: 86 tests, 0 failures after the change (previously 1 failure).

title: The provisioned Keycloak realm issues tokens with NO 'aud' claim - the audience validator is unsatisfiable, and the platform had no client-identity check at all
actual: Measured against the provisioned realm on Keycloak 26.0 (realm created from docker/keycloak/import/ecommerce-realm.json): a USER token (ROPC, client ecommerce-client) carries aud=ABSENT, azp=ecommerce-client, realm_access.roles=[USER]; an ADMIN token carries aud=ABSENT, azp=ecommerce-client, realm_access.roles=[ADMIN,MANAGER]; a service token (client_credentials, client order-service) carries aud=ABSENT, azp=order-service, realm_access.roles=[SERVICE]. The realm declares no clientScopes and no protocolMappers, so no audience mapper exists. The fleet therefore had NO audience and NO client-identity control: any token minted by any client in the realm was accepted by every service and by the gateway. The 'aud' validator already present in BaseSecurityConfig was unsatisfiable - enabling shop.security.expected-audiences would have rejected 100% of the tokens and taken the whole fleet offline.
expected: Each service accepts tokens only from the clients it is meant to serve, and the mechanism must work against the realm as provisioned.
trigger: Any token issued by the realm reaches a service or the gateway.
root_cause: The 'C1 fix' assumed an 'aud' claim that this realm never emits, and the property guarding it was empty everywhere, so the control was inert and its failure mode was hidden.
consequences: No client-to-service separation existed. The only discriminator was the realm role, and the SERVICE role is fleet-wide (see F-041). Additionally, the shipped 'aud' validator was a latent outage landmine: the first operator who followed the documentation and set expected-audiences would have locked every user out.
remediation: Validate the 'azp' claim (the only client discriminator the realm emits) through a new shop.security.expected-client-ids property, wire the same validator into the reactive gateway edge, and document that expected-audiences must stay empty until an audience mapper is added to the realm.
regression_test: BaseSecurityConfigClientIdValidationTest and GatewayJwtSecurityConfigTest assert that a token from an unknown client is rejected and one from an accepted client passes.
remediation_applied: common-security: new expectedClientIds property + azp validator; gateway: new GatewayJwtSecurityConfig with a ReactiveJwtDecoder and an azp validator; common-spring: platform default client-id allow-list.
verification_evidence: Keycloak 26.0 token inspection (aud absent, azp present) + 9 new unit tests across common-security and gateway-service.

title: The SERVICE realm role is a fleet-wide super-privilege: any service client token can call any service's SERVICE-gated endpoint, including capturing or refunding any payment
actual: Every service client in the realm (order-service, rating-service, search-service, product-service, media-service) is granted the single realm role SERVICE. A client_credentials token for order-service carries realm_access.roles=[SERVICE] and is accepted by every @PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('SERVICE','ADMIN')") endpoint in the fleet - for example PaymentController.capture and PaymentController.refund, which take a payment id and have no ownership or caller check, and OrderStatusController's confirm/ship/deliver/cancel. Because the realm emits no audience (F-040), a token cannot be bound to the service it was issued to.
expected: A service token should only be able to invoke the specific operations its owner service needs, and a compromised service secret must not grant fleet-wide administrative power.
trigger: Compromise of any single service client secret, or a service making a call outside its remit.
root_cause: A single coarse SERVICE role is used as the only machine-identity discriminator, with no per-caller binding.
consequences: One leaked service secret (for example order-service's, which the audit found defaulted to the literal 'changeme') grants the ability to capture or refund any payment in the platform, commit any inventory reservation and cancel any order.
remediation: Introduce a per-service role or validate the 'azp' claim per operation so a token is bound to its issuing service, and add an ownership check to the money endpoints. Tracked as follow-up task TSK-041.
regression_test: Required: an integration test asserting that an order-service token cannot call a payment capture for a payment it does not own.
